item.title: Bash: How to Await Multiple Background Processes and Check Individual Exit Statuses
item.description:
“Bash: How to Await Multiple Background Processes and Check Individual Exit Statuses”

How can one effectively manage numerous concurrently running background jobs, ensure the main script waits for all of them, and accurately record the return code from each individual execution?

Here are several proven architectural patterns and solutions for handling this common requirement in shell scripting.

Solution Pattern 1: Storing PIDs and Iterative Waiting (The Explicit Approach)

This pattern involves explicitly capturing the Process ID ($!) immediately after launching each background command and then looping through the collected PIDs to call wait on each one. This allows for checking the exit status ($?) immediately after each wait.

item.title: Effective Shell Scripting: Multiple Program Execution Strategies
item.description:
“Effective Shell Scripting: Multiple Program Execution Strategies”

Several potent techniques exist, each suited for different needs regarding output handling, control flow synchronization, and resource management.

Core Techniques for Parallel Launching

Method 1: Simple Backgrounding with & and Synchronization with wait

item.title: Preventing Deadlocks When Redirecting Process Standard I/O in C#
item.description:
“Preventing Deadlocks When Redirecting Process Standard I/O in C#”

When launching an external process using System.Diagnostics.Process in C# and setting RedirectStandardOutput or RedirectStandardError to true, a common pitfall is encountering deadlocks or the process hanging indefinitely. This typically occurs because the operating system’s internal I/O buffers for the redirected streams become full. The external process blocks waiting to write data, but the parent application is blocked waiting for the process to terminate, creating a classic deadlock scenario.

item.title: Reliable Process Restart Strategies Avoiding PID File Pitfalls
item.description:
“Reliable Process Restart Strategies Avoiding PID File Pitfalls”

When running critical applications, ensuring they automatically recover after an unexpected termination is paramount. Relying on methods that evaluate processes outside the established parent-child hierarchy—such as parsing ps output, utilizing PID files, or relying on external crons for direct process evaluation—introduces significant fragility. UNIX design strongly favors processes waiting only on their direct descendants for robust supervision.

What are the superior, more reliable patterns for creating a self-restarting application monitor?
